claim: TA proteins comprise 3–5% of the eukaryotic membrane proteome.
source: TA proteins comprise 3–5% of the eukaryotic membrane proteome and play essential roles in numerous processes including membrane fusion/fission, vesicular trafficking, protein translocation, quality control, and apoptosis (Beilharz et al., 2003; Hegde and Keenan, 2011; Kalbfleisch et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Beilharz et al., 2003; Hegde and Keenan, 2011; Kalbfleisch et al., 2007).

claim: TA proteins play essential roles in numerous processes including membrane fusion/fission, vesicular trafficking, protein translocation, quality control, and apoptosis.
source: TA proteins comprise 3–5% of the eukaryotic membrane proteome and play essential roles in numerous processes including membrane fusion/fission, vesicular trafficking, protein translocation, quality control, and apoptosis (Beilharz et al., 2003; Hegde and Keenan, 2011; Kalbfleisch et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Beilharz et al., 2003; Hegde and Keenan, 2011; Kalbfleisch et al., 2007).

claim: Modulation of the TMD and basic residues at the extreme C-termini alter the localization of TA proteins to the ER or mitochondria.

claim: Targeting of the Get3•TA complex to the ER and TA insertion into the membrane provides an additional selection filter.

claim: TA proteins with suboptimal TMDs, such as 6AG, dissociate from Get3 more quickly than those with more hydrophobic TMDs.

source: Finally, a four leucine substitution in the Fis1 TMD could compensate for its charged CTE and re-direct Fis1 to the GET pathway (Wang et al., 2010), suggesting that TA localization is specified by a combination of multiple physicochemical properties.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Wang et al., 2010).

claim: TA localization is specified by a combination of multiple physicochemical properties.
source: Finally, a four leucine substitution in the Fis1 TMD could compensate for its charged CTE and re-direct Fis1 to the GET pathway (Wang et al., 2010), suggesting that TA localization is specified by a combination of multiple physicochemical properties.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TMD and CTE properties can compensate for each other.

claim: Selection during the initial substrate loading steps utilizes the difference in binding energy of various TAs for Sgt2 and for Get3.
source: Selection during the initial substrate loading steps utilizes the difference in binding energy of various TAs for Sgt2 and for Get3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing differential binding of TAs to Sgt2 and Get3.

claim: After TA proteins are loaded onto Get3, substrates can further partition between disassembly from Get3 and productive insertion into ER.
source: After TA proteins are loaded onto Get3, substrates can further partition between disassembly from Get3 and productive insertion into ER, during which authentic substrates partition more favorably into the productive insertion reaction compared to suboptimal substrates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the kinetic analysis showing competition between kinsert and knonproductive.

claim: This partitioning is analogous to proofreading mechanisms observed during rejection of near cognate tRNAs by the ribosome.
source: As this partitioning occurs after irreversible ATP hydrolysis on Get3, it is analogous to proofreading mechanisms observed during rejection of near cognate tRNAs by the ribosome (Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001a, 2001b).
evidence: The claim is an analogy supported by citations to published literature (Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001a, 2001b).

claim: The use of multiple, sequential selection steps allows the GET pathway to distinguish TA proteins destined to different organelles while accommodating a variety of amino acid sequences in the substrate protein.
source: Although each mechanism provides a modest discrimination, the use of multiple, sequential selection steps allows the GET pathway to distinguish TA proteins destined to different organelles while accommodating a variety of amino acid sequences in the substrate protein.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing multiple selection steps with modest individual effects.

claim: This principle has been observed with DNA and RNA polymerases, in translation elongation by the ribosome, and in co-translational protein targeting mediated by the signal recognition particle.
source: This principle has been observed with DNA and RNA polymerases (Sydow and Cramer, 2009), in translation elongation by the ribosome (Ogle and Ramakrishnan, 2005; Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001b), and in co-translational protein targeting mediated by the signal recognition particle (Zhang et al., 2010), and may represent a general principle by which key biological processes attain a high degree of fidelity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Sydow and Cramer, 2009; Ogle and Ramakrishnan, 2005; Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001b; Zhang et al., 2010).

claim: Multiple selection steps may represent a general principle by which key biological processes attain a high degree of fidelity.
source: This principle has been observed with DNA and RNA polymerases (Sydow and Cramer, 2009), in translation elongation by the ribosome (Ogle and Ramakrishnan, 2005; Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001b), and in co-translational protein targeting mediated by the signal recognition particle (Zhang et al., 2010), and may represent a general principle by which key biological processes attain a high degree of fidelity.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on observations across multiple systems.

claim: The differences in substrate binding affinity of Get3 may not be fully realized in the GET pathway to generate effective selection due to the high kinetic stability of the Get3•TA interaction.
source: Although the substrate preferences of Get3 parallels those of Sgt2, the differences in substrate binding affinity of Get3 may not be fully realized in the GET pathway to generate effective selection. This is due to the high kinetic stability of the Get3•TA interaction, which dissociates more slowly (τ ~ 30–60 min) than its subsequent targeting and insertion (τ ~ 5–7 min).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of dissociation and insertion timescales.

claim: Sgt2 could help overcome this problem by rejecting a fraction of GET-independent substrates prior to loading onto Get3.
source: Sgt2 could help overcome this problem by rejecting a fraction of GET-independent substrates prior to loading onto Get3.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the kinetic properties of Sgt2 and Get3.

claim: A borderline substrate bound to Sgt2 could more readily equilibrate with alternative machineries in the cytosol than if the same substrate were bound to Get3.
source: As Sgt2 forms less stable complexes with TA proteins than Get3, a borderline substrate bound to Sgt2 could more readily equilibrate with alternative machineries in the cytosol than if the same substrate were bound to Get3 (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the relative stabilities of Sgt2•TA and Get3•TA complexes.

claim: The mammalian Sgt2 homolog, SGTA, associates with the Bag6 complex.
source: The mammalian Sgt2 homolog, SGTA, associates with the Bag6 complex.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Bag6, together with TRC35 and Ubl4A, provides a structural analogue of the Get4/5 complex to mediate TA substrate transfer to TRC40.
source: Although the C-terminal domain of Bag6, together with TRC35 and Ubl4A, provides a structural analogue of the Get4/5 complex to mediate TA substrate transfer to TRC40 (the mammalian Get3 homologue) (Mock et al., 2015), Bag6 also contains additional domains that mediate membrane protein quality control (Hessa et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mock et al., 2015).

claim: Bag6 also contains additional domains that mediate membrane protein quality control.
source: Although the C-terminal domain of Bag6, together with TRC35 and Ubl4A, provides a structural analogue of the Get4/5 complex to mediate TA substrate transfer to TRC40 (the mammalian Get3 homologue) (Mock et al., 2015), Bag6 also contains additional domains that mediate membrane protein quality control (Hessa et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hessa et al., 2011).

claim: Whether the Bag6 complex directs suboptimal TA substrates loaded on SGTA to quality control machineries is an attractive hypothesis that remains to be tested.
source: Whether the Bag6 complex directs suboptimal TA substrates loaded on SGTA to quality control machineries and thus provides such a branch point is an attractive hypothesis that remains to be tested (Lee and Ye, 2013; Leznicki and High, 2012).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations to published literature (Lee and Ye, 2013; Leznicki and High, 2012).

claim: Analogous branches have been suggested by physical interactions between Sgt2 and heatshock proteins in yeast.
source: Analogous branches have been suggested by physical interactions between Sgt2 and heatshock proteins in yeast (Kohl et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2010), but the mechanistic details of these and other machineries await discovery.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kohl et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2010).

claim: The presence of Get4/5 accelerated the TA transfer reaction 5–10 fold.
source: Consistent with the contribution of Get4/5 to TA transfer observed previously (Mateja et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2010), the presence of Get4/5 accelerated the TA transfer reaction 5–10 fold (Figure 6C, grey vs. black, and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Table 2, and citations to published literature (Mateja et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2010).

claim: Rapid TA transfer was observed even when the reaction was carried out in the presence of ribosome-depleted △get3 lysate.
source: Finally, rapid TA transfer was observed even when the reaction was carried out in the presence of ribosome-depleted △get3 lysate (Figure 6D), suggesting that Get4/5-dependent TA transfer is robust and can withstand competition from cellular factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Get4/5-dependent TA transfer is robust and can withstand competition from cellular factors.
source: Finally, rapid TA transfer was observed even when the reaction was carried out in the presence of ribosome-depleted △get3 lysate (Figure 6D), suggesting that Get4/5-dependent TA transfer is robust and can withstand competition from cellular factors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TA transfer occurs efficiently in lysate.

claim: BODIPY-FL-labeled Get3 exhibits translocation and ATPase activities similar to those of wildtype Get3.
source: BODIPY-FL-labeled Get3 (denoted as Get3BDP) exhibits translocation and ATPase activities similar to those of wildtype Get3 (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H,I.
